articles.title: Russia’s LEO Advances Put New Pressure on Europe to Bolster its Space Security - Via Satellite
articles.summary: Russia’s LEO Advances Put New Pressure on Europe to Bolster its Space Security  Via Satellite
articles.full_text:
As Russia begins deploying its military RASSVET constellation, internal political fractures and slow-moving bureaucracy are leaving Europe completely reliant on the U.S. for security in orbit. And things won’t change anytime soon.
Marc C Lange has been following with concern the events surrounding the attempted drone attack on a Ukrainian military plane at the Leipzig/Halle Airport in Germany in August this year. The Berlin-based defense advisor sees these escalating hybrid attacks from Russia as a portent of worse things to come. The incident, since attributed to Russian and Belarusian saboteurs, prompted German politicians to close the Russian consulate in Bonn. Russia denied involvement, calling allegations “absurd” and warned of diplomatic consequences.
A string of other suspicious incidents across Europe quickly followed, including unexplained fires at a military robotics factory in Estonia and a drone manufacturing facility in Poland.
“There are signs that Russia may want to escalate in the next 12 months,” Lange, who is also the author of the Tech Wars newsletter, tells Via Satellite. “There’s a clock ticking for Vladimir Putin to do it. The risk of Russia starting a military operation against Europe has never been greater, and the evidence is raining down on us.”
Lange is most concerned about the fact that despite lofty talk about defense investment, Europe doesn’t seem to be in a rush to close its strategic defense and security technology gaps. This vulnerability, in particular, involves strategic infrastructure in space.
“If somebody east of [Germany] decides to launch a ballistic missile at us, we will not see it unless the United States passes on the intelligence data,” Lange says. “We rely on the U.S. for a lot of these things, and so does Ukraine.”
It’s not just the American Space-Based Infrared System (SBIRS) for early missile warning that Europe needs for its security. When the chief of German military space command Maj. Gen. Michael Traut revealed in February that Russian spy satellites had been eavesdropping on about a dozen European strategic communication spacecraft in Geostationary Orbit (GEO), he knew about the activity only thanks to American space situational awareness providers.
According to the Secure World Foundation’s 2026 Global Counterspace Capabilities Report, both Europe’s defensive and offensive space architecture, lags behind not only the U.S. and China, but also its primary adversary, Russia. That includes electronic warfare systems, such as jammers and spoofers, directed energy weapons such as lasers, and a new generation of co-orbital systems that involve offensive satellites carrying various kinds of interceptors or disruptive systems.
For Lange, the biggest concern at the moment is Ukraine’s dependence on SpaceX’s Starlink megaconstellation for guiding drones around the war zone and for long-range strikes on targets in Russia. No space-based system available in Europe currently supports drone warfare, meaning Europe has nothing to offer Ukraine should it lose access to Starlink in the future.
“Ukraine’s deep strike campaign is running on American intelligence data and Starlink terminals,” says Lange. “The moment one or both of these assets are not available to Ukraine anymore, that campaign ends.”
Russia, too, used to rely on Starlink terminals to guide drones deeper into Ukrainian territory. But earlier this year in February, SpaceX agreed to a registration scheme that allows Ukraine to limit who can use Starlink on its territory, including regions in the east that are currently under Russian control.
The sudden loss of access to Starlink was a setback for Russia, which it is still scrambling to overcome. But Lange warns that Russia’s determination to deploy a domestic military space constellation that would take over the role of Starlink in drone and robotic warfare is vastly outpacing Europe’s efforts to have its own back-up in place. If Russia were to invade an EU country, as many analysts think it might before 2030, it would certainly lean onto the drone and robotic warfare technology that it has perfected during the conflict in Ukraine. The ability to use its own satellites to guide those strikes would give Moscow a distinct advantage. And Moscow certainly knows that.
While Europe is still three years away from the launch of the first batch of satellites for the IRIS² constellation, Russia began launching its RASSVET fleet in March this year and reports cite it already has 32 satellites in orbit. Ukrainian defense intelligence sources told the military intelligence platform Janes that by late July, Russia had been able to use its new satellites to beam connectivity to Ukrainian territory for at least several hours a day. This connectivity could soon provide links to guide drones beyond the reach of standard radio control, possibly hundreds or even thousands of kilometers into the unoccupied lands.
“My impression is that Russia has fully understood the existential necessity of RASSVET,” says Lange.
Despite negative news reports that have recently flagged the problems plaguing RASSVET satellites in orbit, Lange is convinced that Moscow has what it takes to pull the project off.
“If Russia is good at one thing, it is persistence,” he says. “I do not have any doubt that they’re going to continue to build out this capability.”
Samuel Bendett, an analyst at the Center for Naval Research (CNA) who specializes in Russian military technology, tells Via Satellite that Russia sees Rassvet as “a matter of life and death,” with many voices inside the country being highly critical of the past reliance on Starlink.
“They have been developing plans for Rassvet since around 2021,” Bendett notes. “Their original plan was to launch 156 satellites by the end of this year, which is probably not going to happen, and nearly 300 by the end of 2027. They plan to have over 600 satellites in orbit by the end of 2028 and 900 by 2035.”
Bendett stresses that although Russia may be dealing with technical problems and is unlikely to get satellites operational at the projected pace, even a much lower number of spacecraft will provide coverage not just over Ukraine, but over the adjacent territories in Poland and the Baltic states, which are the likeliest target of a future Russian aggression.
Contrast that with Europe. In August, the European Commission announced it was “accelerating” the deployment of IRIS2, with first launches now expected in 2029 (from the initially planned 2030). The Commission also decided to expand the constellation from the originally planned 282 to a total of 348 spacecraft. The constellation might be fully deployed between 2031 and 2032, yet many insiders see this timeline as far too optimistic.
Contracts to build the constellations’ satellites were awarded last month to AerospaceLab and Airbus. AerospaceLab, a newcomer in the field, will produce 264 out of the 348 spacecraft at a cost of around 9.1 million euro ($10.5 million) per satellite, according to Reuters. The company has reportedly built eight satellites for various clients since its conception in 2018. It is currently constructing a satellite “mega-factory” in Charleroi, Belgium.
The fact that the European Commission entrusted a single company, and a relative newcomer, with such a major share of the constellation, in Lange’s eyes, raises concerns. But there are other aspects of the IRIS2 endeavor that suggest Europe may be failing to adapt.
“With IRIS2, the EU is simultaneously trying to do too much and missing the mark on some core important factors,” he says. “This thing reeks of complexity. These satellites contain multiple different communication payloads, PNT payloads, and optional governmental payloads. Europe has decided to go for complex and fancy, and what I would describe as over-engineered. But imagine you were to offer it to Ukraine today? Tell them you can offer them a constellation, it’s super fancy and sophisticated, but it might not be ready before 2035?”
When confronted with the criticism, the European Commission spokesperson told Via Satellite in an email that “Europe is not waiting” and reiterated that the Commission is “accelerating IRIS² and expanding it to 350 satellites, with first launches from 2029.” They stated that IRIS² will boost EU secure government capacity by 60 percent for defense, security and emergency services.”

articles.title: A 3.1 MWh grid battery energized in eastern Wisconsin runs with no cooling system, and its passive sodium ion design outperformed lithium iron phosphate on a 15-state grid - Energies Media
articles.summary: A 3.1 MWh grid battery energized in eastern Wisconsin runs with no cooling system, and its passive sodium ion design outperformed lithium iron phosphate on a 15-state grid  Energies Media
articles.full_text:
In a flat corner of eastern Wisconsin, a steel container the length of a semi trailer was switched on and began pushing electricity onto a live grid.
It stored 3.1 megawatt hours of energy.
It weighed 100,000 pounds fully loaded.
A prior installation at a solar testing facility in Watkins, Colorado stores 3.5 MWh and has been running since 2025, but Watkins was a controlled test environment.
And it had no cooling system at all.
Every lithium iron phosphate battery bolted to this same grid needs one, and cooling is where most of those batteries eventually fail.
So what happens when grid storage is built to run without it?
The cooling problem hiding inside every lithium iron phosphate battery storage site
Lithium iron phosphate cells generate heat when they charge and discharge, and that heat is the enemy of both safety and longevity. Left unmanaged, it accelerates capacity loss and, in the worst cases, triggers thermal runaway: a chain reaction where one hot cell heats its neighbor until the whole pack ignites.
To prevent that, every commercial lithium iron phosphate storage system on American grids runs active cooling equipment, including pumps, fans, refrigerants and control electronics, continuously cycling to keep cells in a safe temperature band. That machinery is expensive to buy, expensive to power, and statistically likely to fail before the batteries themselves do. By removing active cooling components, the Wisconsin system’s designer says it eliminates more than 85 percent of the root causes behind historical battery storage failures.
The key is cell formulation. The system relies on sodium ion phosphate pyrophosphate cells, a chemistry that removes cooling systems, eliminates costly routine maintenance and reduces the excess storage required to account for capacity degradation. Sodium ions are larger and less reactive under thermal stress than lithium ions, and that atomic difference is what makes the passive design possible.
The container in eastern Wisconsin and how it got there
The deployment, energized in March 2026, marks the first time sodium ion batteries have backed up the MISO grid, which serves 15 central US states and the Canadian province of Manitoba. The site is a testing facility operated by the energy company that partnered on the pilot, located outside Milwaukee, and the system arrived as a single containerized unit ready to connect.
The developer described it as the largest sodium ion phosphate pyrophosphate battery system in the world and the first grid scale sodium ion storage solution deployed to the US grid. A prior installation at a solar testing facility in Watkins, Colorado stores 3.5 MWh and has been running since 2025, but Watkins was a controlled test environment. Wisconsin is the MISO interconnection, a live market where the battery must respond to real dispatch signals and deliver on contract, not just on a data sheet.
What the performance numbers actually show
Performance testing indicated the passive design could reduce auxiliary power use by up to 90 percent, saving approximately $1 million annually per gigawatt hour installed compared to lithium iron phosphate systems. That figure comes from the developer’s own testing, not an independent audit, and it should be read as an upper bound rather than a guaranteed outcome in every environment.
Even so, a system that draws no power to cool itself will always run at a lower parasitic load than one that does. The developer describes its maintenance schedule as essentially nonexistent, calling the system simple with no moving parts, no planned maintenance and negligible auxiliary loads. As first reported at the time of the pilot agreement, a separate analysis concluded that installing 10 GWh of battery storage across MISO over the next decade could reduce total system costs by as much as $27 billion, and a grid facing surging demand from data centers and electrification is exactly the market where that cost wedge matters most.
Where the technology hits its limits
Sodium ion cells carry less energy per pound than the best lithium ion alternatives, and that gap matters when storage space is tight. The cell at the core of the latest designs achieves around 160 Wh per kilogram, with 97 percent energy conversion efficiency and more than 15,000 cycles at 80 percent capacity retention. Those are competitive figures for stationary storage, but a lithium ion pack targeting maximum density can still beat them on energy per unit of footprint.
Then there is the supply chain. The cells inside the Wisconsin container were manufactured in China to the developer’s specification and assembled in the US. That arrangement is commercially pragmatic today, but it leaves the cost structure exposed to the same trade disruptions that have already rattled lithium supply chains. The answer the developer is building toward is domestic production: a $71 million factory in Sacramento described as the first US facility dedicated to grid scale sodium ion storage, with shipments expected in early 2027, backed by more than 6 GWh of customer commitments.
What the Wisconsin test means for grids built on lithium assumptions
Every major grid operator in the United States has sized its storage procurement pipelines around lithium iron phosphate. The contracts, the interconnection queue, the fire suppression standards and the utility training programs all assume active cooling as baseline. A passively cooled system does not just swap one chemistry for another; it removes an entire mechanical layer the industry spent a decade learning to manage.
The company has secured more than 6 GWh of customer commitments, including a deal with a leading grid storage developer for up to 4.75 GWh through 2030, valued at up to $500 million. Announced customer interest is approaching $1 billion across data centers, critical infrastructure and utility markets. Advances in unconventional grid storage, from a ceramic squeezed to extreme pressure to the sodium ion box in Wisconsin, share the same ambition: get the grid off its dependence on a handful of expensive, fragile minerals. Innovations built on radical physical simplicity, such as pencil-tube generation from raindrops, point toward the same horizon.
The container does not know any of that. It keeps charging and discharging, cooler free, in a state that sells more cheese than it does batteries.

articles.title: ActivTrak Work Intelligence Covered in New Analyst Report - AOL.com
articles.summary: ActivTrak Work Intelligence Covered in New Analyst Report  AOL.com
articles.full_text:
Report examines how ActivTrak helps organizations assess AI's impact on work and identify opportunities for automation
AUSTIN, Texas, Oct. 7, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- ActivTrak today announced it has been featured in a new industry analyst report on its growing work intelligence capabilities. The report, ActivTrak expands into workflow optimization with Work Intelligence Platform, published by 451 Research, part of S&P Global, examines the company's evolution beyond workforce analytics to provide broader work intelligence across people, process and technology.
The report comes as organizations face growing pressure to demonstrate that investments in AI and automation improve how work actually gets done. According to 451 Research's Voice of the Enterprise: Workforce Productivity & Collaboration, Digital Workplace Decision-Makers 2025 survey, 52% of respondents cited integrating AI and generative AI into workflows as a leading priority for the next 12 months, while 45% selected increasing automation to streamline employee processes.
Against this backdrop, organizations are looking beyond AI adoption to understand its impact on work itself.
"Companies are investing aggressively in AI, but adoption is only the beginning," said Heidi Farris, CEO of ActivTrak. "Leaders need to know where AI and automation can meaningfully improve work, what they should change first and whether those investments actually deliver results. The opportunity is to turn that evidence into a continuous improvement cycle that informs where the business invests and how work evolves over time."
"The progression, from tracking basic AI usage to measuring AI's effect on productivity, cost and output, is central to why Work Intelligence is gaining relevance now," said Ethan Ray, Senior Research Analyst, 451 Research by S&P Global.
ActivTrak provides a continuous view of digital work across applications and transforms behavioral work data into insights, benchmarks, recommendations and measurement. This helps organizations understand workforce capacity and productivity, assess how AI affects work, identify opportunities to improve workflows and automate work, and measure whether changes deliver meaningful business impact.
Turning Work Intelligence Into Workflow Improvement
The new report highlights ActivTrak's expansion into workflow optimization as a significant part of its broader work intelligence strategy. "ActivTrak Workflow turns behavioral work data into work intelligence, revealing where friction, repetitive work and inefficiency affect capacity," writes Ray.
Advertisement
ActivTrak Workflow extends visibility beyond individual applications and predefined processes to reveal work across and between systems. Using aggregated intelligence at the task, role and team level, it helps organizations surface repetitive work, bottlenecks, technology friction and other opportunities for improvement; determine where AI, automation, workflow redesign or other interventions can create value; and measure what changes after action is taken.
The approach is designed for less-structured knowledge work that can be difficult to understand through traditional system data alone. As Ray writes, "Process-mining tools reconstruct detailed event sequences in repeatable, transaction-heavy processes; ActivTrak instead emphasizes continuous discovery across less-structured, cross-application knowledge work."
Putting AI in the Context of Work
The report also highlights how ActivTrak connects AI usage to the broader context of work. Rather than analyze AI in isolation, ActivTrak shows how AI and other technologies fit into the way work gets done — including activity that spans systems and tools adopted outside central procurement.
This cross-application perspective puts AI alongside the other factors that shape capacity, productivity and performance. As a result, leaders gain a clearer view of how technology changes the composition of work itself — including the balance between human work, AI-assisted work and the technologies that connect them.
To learn more:

ActivTrak provides the work intelligence organizations need to understand and improve work in the AI era. Its award-winning technology combines privacy-first behavioral data across people, process and technology to provide a continuous view of how work gets done. This helps leaders measure AI impact, optimize productivity and capacity, identify workflow and automation opportunities, and improve operational performance. ActivTrak is trusted by more than 9,500 organizations worldwide and recognized by Deloitte's Technology Fast 500, Inc. 5000, TrustRadius and G2. The company is backed by Elsewhere Partners, Sapphire Ventures and Francisco Partners. Learn more at www.activtrak.com.

articles.title: Electric Vehicle Test Equipment Market Forecast to Expand Through 2035 as Battery Validation Demand Accelerates - IndexBox
articles.summary: Electric Vehicle Test Equipment Market Forecast to Expand Through 2035 as Battery Validation Demand Accelerates  IndexBox
articles.full_text:
AVL List GmbH
Broad portfolio for EV development
According to the latest IndexBox report on the global Electric Vehicle Test Equipment market, the market enters 2026 with broader demand fundamentals, more disciplined procurement behavior, and a more regionally diversified supply architecture.
The global Electric Vehicle Test Equipment Market is entering a structurally driven expansion phase, with demand fundamentals tied directly to the cadence of EV platform launches, battery pack refreshes, and the build-out of gigafactory production capacity. Unlike conventional automotive tooling markets, this segment is shaped by validation and qualification logic: OEMs and Tier-1 suppliers must demonstrate compliance with UN/ECE R100, ISO 26262, and regional type-approval regimes, which mandates specific test hardware, software, and data traceability.
The market is bifurcating into high-value, low-volume R&D and validation systems for new platform development, and cost-optimized, high-throughput production testers for battery and powertrain lines. This divergence creates distinct competitive dynamics, sales cycles, and pricing architectures. Demand is program-driven and therefore lumpy, but the direction through 2035 is upward as EV penetration rises, charging infrastructure expands, and aftermarket diagnostic needs emerge. Suppliers that can deliver integrated, software-enabled validation solutions and maintain engineering proximity to OEM R&D hubs and gigafactory clusters are best positioned to capture value.
The forecast horizon 2026-2035 points to sustained growth, with the market index reaching 178 by 2035 from a 2025 base of 100, equivalent to a 5.9% CAGR.
The baseline scenario for the Electric Vehicle Test Equipment Market through 2035 assumes continued global EV adoption, steady platform launches, and progressive tightening of safety and performance standards. Under this scenario, the market expands at a 5.9% CAGR from 2025 to 2035, with the market index rising from 100 in 2025 to 178 in 2035. Growth is not linear: capital expenditure on test equipment follows OEM program cycles, creating periods of accelerated ordering around new platform starts and battery chemistry transitions, followed by consolidation phases.
The R&D and validation segment remains the highest-value pool, driven by the need for high-fidelity simulation, environmental testing, and functional safety verification. The production test segment grows faster in unit terms as gigafactory capacity expands, particularly in Asia-Pacific and North America, but faces greater price pressure and shorter replacement cycles. Software and services become an increasing share of supplier revenue, with recurring income from calibration, data analytics, and over-the-air test sequence updates. Geographically, Asia-Pacific retains the largest share, supported by China's EV production scale and battery supply chain depth.
North America and Europe grow robustly as localization incentives and stricter emissions rules spur regional capacity. Latin America and the Middle East & Africa remain smaller but offer niche opportunities in aftermarket diagnostics and fleet electrification. Key risks to the baseline include slower-than-expected EV demand, supply chain constraints for high-power components, and engineering talent shortages, which could delay equipment deliveries and inflate costs.
Battery testing and validation represents the largest and most critical segment of the Electric Vehicle Test Equipment Market. Demand is driven by the need to verify cell, module, and pack performance under extreme conditions, including thermal runaway, cycle life, and fast-charging protocols. As battery chemistries evolve toward higher nickel and solid-state variants, test regimes become more complex, requiring equipment capable of precise voltage and current control, environmental simulation, and data traceability. The segment is bifurcating: R&D labs demand high-fidelity, flexible systems for characterization, while gigafactories require high-throughput testers for end-of-line verification.
Through 2035, the shift to 800V architectures and faster charging will necessitate upgraded test equipment, and regulatory pressures will mandate more rigorous safety testing. Demand-side indicators include battery production volume, new battery plant announcements, and the rate of chemistry innovation. Suppliers must offer scalable solutions that bridge R&D and production, with software that can adapt to evolving test standards. Current trend: Increasing share due to battery safety and performance requirements.
Major trends: Rising demand for solid-state battery testing, Integration of AI for predictive battery analytics, Shift to 800V and higher voltage testing, Modular test systems for flexibility, and Increased focus on thermal runaway testing.
Representative participants: AVL List GmbH, Chroma ATE Inc, Keysight Technologies, Horiba Ltd, and National Instruments.
Powertrain and e-motor testing covers the validation of electric drive units, inverters, and integrated powertrain systems. As OEMs move toward dedicated EV platforms, the need for comprehensive testing of power electronics, thermal management, and NVH characteristics intensifies. Test equipment must simulate real-world driving conditions, including torque and speed profiles, while ensuring functional safety and reliability. The segment is experiencing a shift from component-level testing to system-level validation, requiring dynamometers and test benches that can handle higher power densities and faster switching frequencies. Through 2035, the rise of multi-motor configurations and in-wheel motors will create new test challenges.
Demand indicators include the number of new e-powertrain programs, production volumes of electric drive units, and the adoption of wide-bandgap semiconductors. Suppliers that can provide integrated test solutions with real-time simulation and data analytics will gain advantage. Current trend: Steady growth driven by powertrain electrification and integration.
Major trends: System-level testing replacing component testing, Adoption of SiC and GaN semiconductors, Multi-motor and in-wheel motor testing, NVH and thermal management validation, and Real-time simulation integration.
Representative participants: AVL List GmbH, Horiba Ltd, Keysight Technologies, DEKRA, and TÜV SÜD.
Charging system and infrastructure testing is a fast-growing segment, driven by the global build-out of EV charging networks and the need to ensure interoperability, safety, and performance. Test equipment is used to validate AC and DC chargers, vehicle-to-grid (V2G) communication, and connector durability. As charging speeds increase toward 350 kW and beyond, test systems must handle higher power levels and complex communication protocols. Regulatory standards such as ISO 15118 and regional mandates for charger certification are key demand drivers. Through 2035, the proliferation of wireless charging and bidirectional charging will create new test requirements.
Demand indicators include the number of public charging points, investment in charging infrastructure, and the rate of standard updates. Suppliers must offer test solutions that cover the entire charging ecosystem, from grid to vehicle, with automated test sequences and cybersecurity validation. Current trend: Rapid growth due to charging infrastructure expansion and interoperability requirements.
Major trends: High-power DC charging testing, V2G and bidirectional charging validation, Wireless charging test development, Cybersecurity and communication protocol testing, and Interoperability certification.
Representative participants: Keysight Technologies, Chroma ATE Inc, TÜV SÜD, DEKRA, and SGS S.A.
Vehicle integration and system testing involves the validation of complete EVs, including electrical architecture, software, and subsystem interactions. This segment is driven by the increasing complexity of vehicle electronics, over-the-air updates, and the need to ensure functional safety across all systems. Test equipment includes hardware-in-the-loop (HIL) simulators, network analyzers, and environmental chambers. As OEMs adopt zonal architectures and central computing, testing must cover a wider range of scenarios, from electromagnetic compatibility to cybersecurity. Through 2035, the rise of autonomous driving features will further integrate ADAS testing with EV system validation.
Demand indicators include the number of new EV models, software content per vehicle, and the adoption of new communication standards like Automotive Ethernet. Suppliers that can provide scalable HIL and integration test platforms will benefit. Current trend: Moderate growth as vehicle-level validation becomes more complex.
Major trends: Hardware-in-the-loop simulation growth, Zonal architecture testing, Cybersecurity and OTA validation, EMC testing for high-voltage systems, and Integration with ADAS testing.
Representative participants: National Instruments, Keysight Technologies, AVL List GmbH, Horiba Ltd, and Element Materials Technology.
Aftermarket diagnostics and service is a nascent but promising segment, driven by the growing EV parc and the need for cost-effective diagnostic tools for repair shops and service centers. Unlike OEM-focused capital equipment, aftermarket tools must be affordable, portable, and easy to use, with capabilities for battery state-of-health assessment, fault code reading, and component testing. As EVs age, battery degradation and electronic failures will create demand for diagnostic equipment that can quickly identify issues and support repair decisions. Through 2035, the aftermarket segment will expand as warranties expire and independent repair networks gain capability.

articles.title: Starlink ready to launch India services, awaits final government approval - Madhyamam
articles.summary: Starlink ready to launch India services, awaits final government approval  Madhyamam
articles.full_text:
Starlink ready to launch India services, awaits final government approval
text_fields
New Delhi: Elon Musk-led satellite communications company Starlink is hopeful of receiving the final approvals from the Indian government soon to begin operations in the country, a senior company executive said on Wednesday.
Starlink Business Operations vice-president Lauren Dreyer said the company was ready to work with India and had built its operations specifically to meet the country’s security requirements and regulations.
“We have built our Starlink operations specifically for India in recognition of Indian security requirements and other regulations, establishing controls at every layer for India and keeping Indian user data within India,” Dreyer said at the India Mobile Congress 2026 in New Delhi.
She said Starlink had already made investments and set up ground infrastructure in India, including 20 gateway sites with hundreds of antennas.
“We have established the operations to be ready to serve India,” she said.
Expressing hope that the pending approvals would be completed soon, Dreyer said: “Hopefully, next time I address the Congress, the government’s work will be complete, and Starlink will be authorised and ready.”
The company has been preparing for the Indian market for the past five years, keeping the country’s security requirements in mind while setting up its operations. It has also signed memorandums of understanding with Airtel and Jio as part of its preparations to serve customers in India.
Dreyer said Starlink had been building relationships in India and engaging with regulators over the past five years.
She noted that India had already achieved large-scale connectivity through affordable data and a fast-growing digital economy, but the last mile remained the most difficult area to connect.
“It’s also where Starlink offers the biggest potential to help accelerate the speed to connect 100 per cent of India,” she said.
Starlink is awaiting security clearance from the Indian government and approval for foreign direct investment. The company has already received clearances from IN-SPACe and the Global Mobile Personal Communication by Satellite licence.
“We are standing ready to serve India once India is ready. We’re ready to work with the government, with operators and with industry to this end,” Dreyer said.
She added that Starlink was ready to help Prime Minister Narendra Modi achieve his vision of 100 per cent connectivity across India, a goal she said the company, including Musk, shared.
Dreyer also referred to Starlink’s engagement with India’s space sector, saying SpaceX and India had been working together. She highlighted the company’s role in carrying Indian astronaut Shubhanshu Shukla to and from the International Space Station.
(Inputs from IANS)

articles.title: Korea Puts Five Microsatellites Into Orbit in One Launch - Seoul Economic Daily
articles.summary: Korea Puts Five Microsatellites Into Orbit in One Launch  Seoul Economic Daily
articles.full_text:
Five microsatellites that reached orbit aboard the Nuri rocket on the 7th will monitor the Korean Peninsula in near real time for the next three years. The government plans to launch the remaining five NEONSAT satellites next September, completing South Korea's first mass-produced satellite constellation.
The NEONSAT 2 through 6 satellites lifted off at 12:25 p.m. on the 7th, according to the Korea AeroSpace Administration and the Korea Aerospace Research Institute. Each weighs less than 100 kilograms. By comparison, the Compact Advanced Satellite 500-3 launched on the fourth Nuri rocket last year weighed about 516 kilograms, meaning the new satellites are less than one-fifth the weight of that mid-size craft.
What sets the system apart is not size but frequency: multiple satellites operate as a single network, allowing far more frequent observation. Constellation operations have spread quickly across the global space industry, as seen in SpaceX's Starlink, which links thousands of small communications satellites into one network. "The global trend is to build many small, inexpensive satellites to carry out a mission rather than relying on a single large one," said Oh Tae-seok, administrator of the Korea AeroSpace Administration. "A constellation system assumes that 10% of microsatellites may fail, and is designed so the group as a whole can still complete its mission even if some satellites run into trouble."
To that end, the government will launch NEONSAT 7 through 11 next September. NEONSAT 1 went into orbit in April 2024. An official at the space agency said the constellation can photograph the area around the Korean Peninsula quickly and across a wide area, adding that a 10-satellite constellation can capture high-volume imagery covering 700,000 square kilometers.
Once complete, the constellation is expected to meet most of the public sector's demand for satellite imagery, sharply reducing spending on imagery purchased from abroad. Operating the satellites over regions beyond the Korean Peninsula could also generate revenue in the overseas market for high-resolution imagery at sub-meter resolution.
The satellites are also expected to work in tandem with existing high-resolution reconnaissance assets, strengthening round-the-clock surveillance of key targets. The imagery can be used for natural disasters such as typhoons, floods, earthquakes and wildfires. "How quickly and how cheaply you can build microsatellites will become a critical capability," Oh said. "This fifth Nuri launch has opened the country's first era of mass-produced microsatellites and constellations, and we will work to keep launches going on a regular basis."

articles.title: India Moves To Cut China Dependence In Rare Earth Magnet Supply - Electronics For You BUSINESS
articles.summary: India Moves To Cut China Dependence In Rare Earth Magnet Supply  Electronics For You BUSINESS
articles.full_text:
India is building domestic rare earth magnet capacity as Shaktikanta Das highlights China’s 80–90% supply dominance and its risks for electronics manufacturing.
India is moving to build domestic capacity for rare-earth permanent magnets, a critical input for electronic hardware and automobile manufacturing, as the government seeks to reduce vulnerabilities arising from dependence on China.
Shaktikanta Das, Principal Secretary-2 to the Prime Minister, said the government responded to global supply-chain vulnerabilities by launching a major initiative to develop domestic rare-earth magnet capacity.
“The central government came out immediately thereafter with a major initiative to develop domestic capacity in rare earth permanent magnets,” Das said.
Highlighting the importance of these magnets to electronics manufacturing, he said, “Because that is one critical component on which automobile manufacturing, electronic hardware manufacturing, and so much other manufacturing depends.”
Das said China’s dominance of the rare-earth magnet ecosystem had exposed a major global supply-chain vulnerability. “China had imposed certain restrictions. It was a problem for almost the whole world, and because almost 80 to 90 per cent of rare earth magnet supply and that entire ecosystem originates in China,” he said.
The move is part of a broader effort to strengthen India’s control over strategically important manufacturing inputs. China’s Ministry of Commerce expanded rare-earth export controls in October 2025, covering specified permanent magnet materials and components, including samarium-cobalt magnets and certain neodymium magnets containing terbium or dysprosium, Reuters reported.
The controls also covered certain advanced semiconductor-related items and AI research with potential military applications.
For India’s electronics sector, domestic rare-earth magnet capacity could help address a critical supply-chain dependency exposed by China’s export restrictions.

articles.title: Nvidia Nears $6 Trillion Market Value, Deutsche Bank Issues Warning - RS Web Solutions
articles.summary: Nvidia Nears $6 Trillion Market Value, Deutsche Bank Issues Warning  RS Web Solutions
articles.full_text:
On Monday, the Nasdaq achieved an unprecedented closing high, approaching a $6 trillion valuation for Nvidia, as long-term bond yields surged to heights not seen since 2007. Deutsche Bank cautions that this disparity between asset classes cannot continue indefinitely.
Wall Street commenced the week with a notable contradiction. The Nasdaq Composite surged approximately 1% to reach a historic closing peak, while the S&P 500 appreciated by roughly 0.7% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average increased by about 0.2%. Nvidia, renowned as the premier chipmaker globally, also attained a record high, drawing nearer to the elusive $6 trillion market capitalization.
Concurrently, the bond market is emitting cautionary signals. US 10-year Treasury yields ascended to about 5.3% in the previous week—the highest level since 2007—while the 30-year yields approached 5.6%.
In Europe, the differential between the French and German 10-year yields marked its most significant weekly rise in over thirty years.
According to Deutsche Bank, the two markets are forecasting markedly divergent futures. The bank posits that the bond market is indicating a new era characterized by multi-decade-high yields, accelerated interest rate hikes, and oil prices exceeding $100 per barrel.
In stark contrast, equities, credit markets, and the VIX volatility index exhibit minimal stress. Deutsche Bank asserts that while the bond market has integrated these warnings, risk assets have not yet accepted the ramifications.
Nvidia’s magnificent rally elucidates the resilience of the headline indices. Investors are banking on a robust earnings narrative fueled by AI demand, with revenues doubling during the company’s most recent quarter.
This momentum was bolstered on Monday by a $150 billion enhancement of its share buyback initiative and an upgrade from Morgan Stanley.
The larger semiconductor sector has also demonstrated vigor. Micron recently surpassed expectations and elevated its forecast, reporting revenues of $54.23 billion and estimating approximately $61.5 billion for the forthcoming quarter, prompting several analysts to adjust their price targets upwards.
Nonetheless, not all chip manufacturers are thriving; Intel shares experienced a decline following Elon Musk’s confirmation that TSMC is negotiating to join Terafab, the Texas-based chip venture previously solely partnered with Intel.
Analysts observe that the rally has been somewhat insular. Investment continues to gravitate towards the AI and technology infrastructure sectors, often to the detriment of other market segments particularly vulnerable to rising interest rates.
Relief emanated from the labor market. In September, payrolls climbed by a mere 29,000—far beneath the anticipated 84,000 and a significant drop from August’s 162,000.
This shortfall tempered expectations for a Federal Reserve interest rate hike in October, contributing to the S&P 500’s 0.74% ascent on Friday.
Kyle Rodda, a senior financial market analyst at Capital.com, indicated that this rally, again, was driven by technology, as a slight alleviation of interest-rate uncertainties and diminished geopolitical tensions, along with softer crude prices, allowed investors to concentrate on the remarkable earnings growth exhibited by AI firms.
Yet, the bond market did not fully participate in the jubilant atmosphere. Deutsche Bank noted that U.S. stocks initially surged in response to softer inflation data last week, only to retract in the final trading moments as long-term and real yields persisted in their upward trajectory.
The rationale is uncomplicated: Increased real yields elevate the discount rate applied to future profits, significantly affecting firms whose valuations hinge on anticipated growth occurring years ahead.
Prominent technology stocks epitomize this scenario, rendering them particularly susceptible to reevaluation as yields remain high.
The concentration heightens risk. A select few mega-cap stocks prop up the headline indices; hence, a downturn in these key names would adversely impact benchmarks, even if the broader market remains steady.
Deutsche Bank foresees that if this gap narrows through a risk-off sentiment, the U.S. dollar would likely appreciate while the euro and higher-beta currencies could face downward pressure.
Oil retains its status as an unpredictable element. Amin Nasser, CEO of Saudi Aramco, cautioned that replenishing dwindling global inventories might require up to two years, even after full reopening of the Strait of Hormuz.
A fresh supply shock, with inventories this depleted, could amplify inflation expectations and bond yields precisely when equities appear least equipped to absorb such shocks.
The pivotal question for investors remains whether yields will recede or equities will falter. A persistent decline in yields would reinforce the equity rally and bolster the AI narrative.
Conversely, a further uptick in yields would challenge the sustainability of earnings strength in alleviating elevated capital costs.
The S&P 500 concluded last week roughly 1% beneath its record close of 7,798.99 set on August 13, rendering it sufficiently proximate to new highs that any favorable news regarding inflation or oil could propel it past such levels.
However, with the 10-year yield nearing its highest point since before the global financial crisis, the margin for error is notably narrow.
The broader market landscape on Tuesday, October 6, 2026, is characterized by a stark division between equities and bonds.
On Wall Street, the Nasdaq Composite closed at a record high on Monday following a gain of about 1%, with the S&P 500 rising approximately 0.7% and the Dow Jones Industrial Average increasing by about 0.2%, as Nvidia reached unprecedented levels.
In the bond domain, US 10-year Treasury yields recently peaked at their highest since 2007, the UK 30-year gilt yield briefly surpassed 6% on October 1 for the first time since 1998, and the French-German 10-year spread expanded beyond 140 basis points. articles.title: Fastest-Ever ‘Mind Reading’ AI Model Can Reconstruct Images From Your Brain - PetaPixel
articles.summary: Fastest-Ever ‘Mind Reading’ AI Model Can Reconstruct Images From Your Brain  PetaPixelAn AI “mind-reading” tool can reconstruct what you’re looking at from a brain scan  MIT Technology ReviewPsychic AI can read minds — and recreate our thoughts with frightening accuracy: ‘Sci-fi can come true’  New York PostMind-reading tech aims to make AI actually intelligent  New AtlasNew AI Can Figure Out What You’re Thinking About From a Brain Scan  Futurism
articles.full_text:
Scientists have developed an AI model that can “read” a person’s brain activity and reconstruct what they’re looking at with striking speed and accuracy. The astonishing results can be seen above — with the original image that the person sees on the left and the AI’s reconstruction on the right.
The AI model, which is called Brain-IT, was developed in the lab of Prof. Michal Irani at the Weizmann Institute of Science. Brain-IT has been trained to recognize similar patterns of brain activity that occur in different people when they look at images. Unlike earlier AI models, it can then recreate those images with a high level of accuracy, completing the process in about an hour instead of the several hours previously required.
“There exist nowadays models that translate brain activity into images, and they can even produce impressive reconstructions that preserve the semantic meaning of the image reasonably well,” Irani says in a statement. “However, they tend to make mistakes in basic features such as composition and color.”
Irani explains: “The new model we developed outperforms them in reconstructing both the content of the image and its details. What’s more, while every other model requires dozens of hours of brain scans to learn to ‘read’ a new person, our model needs only one hour.”
Researchers trained the system using more than 70,000 images shown to eight people while their brains were scanned. Because eight people is a relatively small dataset for this kind of research, they developed an “encoder” that could identify patterns shared across different people’s brains and predict brain activity from an image.
To build the encoder, the researchers divided each brain scan into about 40,000 tiny sections, called voxels, and measured how each responded to different images. They also used AI to identify visual features in those images, such as colors and locations, as well as what the images depicted, such as faces or food.
By comparing these features with brain activity across the eight participants, they were able to identify patterns that appeared across different brains, despite individual brains responding differently. The researchers found that these shared patterns could be grouped into 128 functional regions involved in processing images.
“During training, the encoder naturally identified 128 functional regions that are shared by all people and perform specific roles in image processing,” Irani explains. “Some of them are familiar to neuroscientists, but others are entirely new. For example, we discovered a division of roles within the brain region that processes images of places – the PPA – with one part responding to indoor scenes and another to outdoor scenes.
According to a report by MIT Technology Review, the team then used the encoder alongside a “decoder” to see whether these patterns could be used to reconstruct images from brain activity. The encoder predicts what a person’s brain activity should look like when they view a particular image, while the decoder works in the opposite direction, using brain activity to reconstruct the image. By repeatedly training the two models together, the researchers were able to make the reconstructions increasingly accurate.
The researchers say the technology behind Brain-IT could eventually help people with paralysis communicate and give scientists a more efficient way to study how the brain processes images.

articles.title: Microsoft Launches $2,599 Surface Laptop Ultra to Take on MacBook Pro - MacRumors
articles.summary: Microsoft Launches $2,599 Surface Laptop Ultra to Take on MacBook Pro  MacRumorsPre-order our most powerful Surface devices ever  Windows BlogMicrosoft debuts Nvidia-powered Surface Laptop Ultra, as it aims for AI market  Yahoo FinanceMicrosoft event debuts new AI-friendly hardware and Windows changes  Ars TechnicaHow Microsoft built its MacBook Pro competitor  The Verge
articles.full_text:
Microsoft today announced launch timing and pricing for the Surface Laptop Ultra that it unveiled earlier this year.
The 15-inch Surface Laptop Ultra is priced starting at $2,599, undercutting Apple's $2,999 16-inch MacBook Pro, and it targets the same creator and developer market. Microsoft says it is built for "demanding creative, software development, AI, engineering, and 3D workloads."
Microsoft's new laptop uses an Nvidia RTX Spark chip, which includes an Nvidia Blackwell RTX GPU with up to 6,144 cores and an Nvidia Grace CPU with up to 20 cores. It supports up to 128GB of unified memory and has a new thermal architecture to support the hardware. The RTX Spark is an Arm-based chip, so the laptop runs Windows on Arm with x86 apps using Microsoft's Prism emulation.
According to Microsoft, the Surface Laptop Ultra is its most powerful notebook to date. It has the "brightest, sharpest, and most vivid display" Microsoft has used in a Surface device, with peak HDR brightness that's 25% higher than the M5 MacBook Pro's. The mini-LED display is a touchscreen, and it supports gestures and navigation, but not pen input.
The laptop is lighter than the 16-inch MacBook Pro, with a large haptic trackpad and upgradeable storage. Microsoft even adopted a MagSafe equivalent, adding support for Magnetic Connect. Microsoft says Magnetic Connect is the "world's first built-in magnetic USB-C charging on a laptop." The device has three USB-C ports, a USB-A port, an HDMI port, an SD card reader, and a 3.5mm headphone jack.
Along with the Surface Laptop Ultra, Microsoft announced the $5,999 Surface RTX Spark Dev Box to compete with devices like the Mac Studio and Mac mini. It is equipped with an Nvidia RTX Spark chip and offers up to 1 petaflop of AI performance with support for AI models up to 120B parameters.
Microsoft is offering a bonus to customers who "break up" with their MacBooks. MacBook owners can get up to $1,000 cash back when purchasing a Surface Laptop Ultra by trading in an eligible MacBook. The Surface Laptop Ultra launches on October 16.
"We're confident that once today's creators and developers experience everything Surface Laptop Ultra has to offer, they won't look back," reads Microsoft's website.
The Surface Laptop Ultra will directly compete with Apple's rumored OLED MacBook, which could also have an Ultra name. The MacBook Ultra is expected to feature a touchscreen, M5 Pro and M5 Max chips, and a thinner and lighter design.

articles.title: Structural basis for regulating lipopolysaccharide transmembrane transport
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-11129-8Structures of the protein machinery in Gram-negative bacteria that transports lipopolysaccharide (LPS) from the cytoplasmic membrane to the outer leaflet of the outer membrane reveal how conformational changes in response to the presence of LPS promote its transport.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Gram-negative bacteria are surrounded by a multilayered cell envelope with a mostly impermeable outer membrane that provides intrinsic resistance to many antibiotics1,2,3,4,5. The outer membrane is an asymmetrical bilayer with phospholipids in the inner leaflet and lipopolysaccharide (LPS) in the outer leaflet6,7. An LPS transport (Lpt) machine called LptB2FGCADE moves LPS across a protein bridge from the inner membrane to the outer membrane8,9. LPS biosynthesis is regulated to prevent toxic accumulation of LPS molecules in the inner membrane during growth10,11,12. Whether LPS transport across the Lpt bridge is also regulated has been unclear. Here we present three structures of the trans-envelope Lpt complex in LPS-free, LPS-bound and ATP-bound states, along with a structure of a partial bridge. These structures, combined with biochemical experiments, show that Lpt bridge assembly triggers movement of the transmembrane helix of LptC (TM-LptC) in an LPS-dependent manner, resulting in increased ATP binding and hydrolysis. We also show that LPS transport in vivo requires bridge formation and movement of the TM-LptC. Our data support a model in which assembled Lpt bridges respond to the presence of LPS in the inner membrane to turn on transport by moving the TM-LptC, thus coordinating LPS transport activity with bridge assembly and the presence of LPS at the inner membrane.
Similar content being viewed by others
Main
Bacterial cells have an inner (cytoplasmic) membrane (IM) containing protein machines that assemble other cell-envelope layers, such as the peptidoglycan cell wall. Gram-negative bacteria also have an outer membrane (OM) that surrounds the peptidoglycan cell wall1,2. This OM has a phospholipid inner leaflet and an LPS outer leaflet6,7. The LPS layer of the OM excludes many antibiotics that are effective against Gram-positive bacteria, greatly limiting therapeutic strategies to treat Gram-negative infections4,5.
LPS is synthesized at the IM and must be transported across the aqueous periplasm and through the OM to the cell surface3. The LPS transport (Lpt) machinery consists of an IM ABC transporter complex (LptB2FGC), an OM translocon (LptDE) and a soluble periplasmic protein (LptA)13,14,15,16,17,18,19,20,21 (Fig. 1a). During the transport of LPS to the cell surface, LptA assembles with the two membrane complexes, forming a continuous trans-envelope protein bridge (LptB2FGCADE)22. LptB2FGCADE uses the energy from ATP binding and hydrolysis in the cytoplasm to extract LPS from the IM and transport it against its concentration gradient directly to the outer leaflet of the OM22,23,24,25,26,27.
A key requirement for LPS transport is that newly synthesized LPS must be transported to the OM efficiently to prevent toxic build-up of LPS at the IM. One mechanism of controlling cellular LPS levels is to turn off LPS biosynthesis10,11. Regulation of the rate of LPS transport would provide an alternative strategy to control IM LPS levels, but it has been unclear whether such regulation occurs.
The rate of LPS transport depends on how many bridges exist and whether they are in an active state. Two types of LptB2FGCADE bridge with different lifetimes have been observed in cells, and we have proposed that only the longer-lived bridges actively transport LPS28. Reducing the levels of LPS decreases the fraction of Lpt components that form assembled bridges in cells, which implies that bridge assembly depends on LPS28. However, the mechanism that underlies the formation of active bridges has been unclear. Here we present three distinct structures of the assembled Lpt bridge, together with a structure of a partial bridge. These structures, combined with biochemistry, reveal the molecular mechanisms that control the formation of active Lpt bridges.
Stabilization of assembled Lpt bridges
To obtain a structure of the full Lpt bridge, we first attempted to isolate intact bridges directly from cells, but the assembled bridges dissociated during purification (Supplementary Fig.
1).
We therefore sought to reconstitute the bridge in vitro from separately purified subcomplexes.
We have previously shown that a variant of the IM subcomplex in which LptA is fused to LptC as a single polypeptide joined by a flexible poly-glycine-serine linker (hereafter termed LptC–LptA fusion) is able to form Lpt bridges28.
Bridges formed with the IM subcomplex containing the LptC–LptA fusion (hereafter termed LptB2FGCA) are more stable in cells than are wild-type bridges, so allowed us to avoid the tendency of soluble LptA to oligomerize when assembling Lpt bridges in vitro18,28,29 (Extended Data Fig.
1a).
We confirmed that the LptC–LptA fusion allows growth on minimal medium in the absence of native LptC and LptA (Extended Data Fig.
1b–d) and assessed the activity of LptB2FGCA through in vivo and in vitro assays.
We observe in vivo site-specific cross-linking of the LptC–LptA fusion to LPS at positions known to cross-link LPS in the individual proteins (Extended Data Fig.
1e).
The ATPase activity of LptB2FGCA in proteoliposomes is similar to that of LptB2FGC (Extended Data Fig.
1f) and we used a flow-cytometry-based assay to confirm that LptB2FGCA can form bridges with LptDE in vitro without the addition of soluble LptA (refs.
22,30; Extended Data Fig.
1g and Supplementary Fig.
2).
Thus, LptB2FGCA recapitulates the functions of the individual LptC and LptA proteins both in vivo and in biochemical assays.

We also stabilized the interface between LptD and LptA by site-specifically incorporating the photocrosslinkable amino acid p-benzoyl-l-phenylalanine (pBPA) at position Y63 in the N-terminal domain of LptD. This site has been shown to cross-link to LptA with high efficiency31. We separately purified LptB2FGCA and LptD(Y63pBPA)E in detergent and co-incubated the purified complexes while exposing to ultraviolet (UV) light. We detected high-efficiency cross-link formation, enabling purification of the full bridge by size-exclusion chromatography (SEC) (Supplementary Fig. 3). We prepared samples for cryo-electron microscopy (cryo-EM) using the purified, covalently stabilized bridge (LptB2FGCAD(Y63pBPA)E; hereafter, LptB2FGCADE).
We observed dumbbell-shaped particles, consistent with two connected membrane complexes (Fig.
1b and Extended Data Fig.
2).
The two-dimensional (2D) class averages showed that the angle between the IM protein complex and the bridge is variable (Fig.
1c), indicating a high degree of flexibility in this region.
The flexibility limited our ability to simultaneously resolve the IM and OM portions of the Lpt bridge to high resolution.
We therefore performed local refinements focused on the region of the structure comprising either LptB2FGC or LptADE starting from a consensus map of the LptB2FGCADE bridge (Extended Data Fig.
2).
These refinements yielded a 3.
3-Å-resolution density map for the IM portion and a 3.
4-Å-resolution density map for the OM region of LptB2FGCADE.
We integrated these local refinements into the consensus map to construct a composite density map (Fig.
1d) for the Lpt bridge and built a model corresponding to this composite map (Fig.
1e).
The periplasmic domains of LptFG (LptF residues 137–246; LptG residues 142–244) remained poorly resolved in the composite map because of flexible connections to their respective TM regions and were therefore not modelled.
We speculate that the observed flexibility of the LptFG periplasmic domains in bridges could be required to allow the formation of a trans-envelope complex (results of three-dimensional (3D) variability analysis are shown in Supplementary Fig.
4 and Supplementary Video 1).
Proteins in the OM are mostly immobile, whereas IM proteins can laterally diffuse freely32,33.
Thus, the flexibility we observe could afford LptB2FGC a range of 2D motion in the IM to move relative to LptDE without breaking the bridge.

Structure of the LptB2FGCADE bridge
The Lpt trans-envelope complex is an elongated structure, approximately 280 Å in length from edge to edge of the membrane complexes (Fig.
1d).
There is clear density corresponding to a LPS molecule bound in the lumen formed by the TM helices of LptFG (hereafter, LptFG lumen; Fig.
1d, panels 7 and 8).
The periplasmic domain is approximately 150 Å in length, somewhat shorter than the estimated periplasmic dimension for Escherichia coli34 (180–240 Å).
It is possible that Lpt bridges in vivo incorporate more than one copy of LptA (approximately 40 Å), although our data indicate that the LptC–LptA fusion with no free LptA is viable (Extended Data Fig.
1b–d).
The structure shows that the IM and OM complexes are connected by the β-jellyroll domains of LptF, LptC, LptA and LptD, which assemble to form a groove that spirals slightly8,18,35,36 (Fig.
1f).
We propose that the spiralling groove serves to minimize clashes between the oligosaccharide portions of adjacent LPS molecules as they are being trafficked.
Cross-sections perpendicular to the long axis of the groove show variability in the space available to accommodate the LPS substrate (Fig.
1d, panels 1–6).
A representation of the internal volume of the periplasm chute calculated with pyKVFinder37 is shown in Extended Data Fig.
3.
The concave surface of the groove is lined predominantly with hydrophobic residues, consistent with the idea that this groove accommodates the acyl chains of LPS during transit to the OM.
However, we observe some constriction points in the chute, with insufficient volume to allow passage of LPS.
Thus, conformational flexibility in the periplasmic domains must be required to allow LPS transport.

The TM helices of LptF and LptG and the bound LPS molecule are well resolved in our local refinement of the LptB2FGC portion of the Lpt bridge, but we did not detect density for the TM helix of LptC (TM-LptC), which suggests that the TM-LptC is not ordered in our structure of the Lpt bridge bound to LPS (Fig. 1d,e). articles.title: Hydrogen bonding in water under extreme confinement
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 07 October 2026; doi:10.1038/s41586-026-10858-0A new technique allows direct nanoscale observations of the vibrational response of water confined inside carbon nanotubes, revealing that high degrees of confinement disrupt the hydrogen bond network through a fluctuating and highly-dispersed molecular state.
articles.full_text:
Abstract
Fluids under extreme confinement or near interfaces exhibit molecular structures and intermolecular bonding distinct from their bulk analogues. Optical vibrational studies have shown that interfacial and confined water can exhibit altered intramolecular O–H stretching frequencies, a sensitive spectral signature of changes in intermolecular hydrogen bonding1,2,3,4. Investigating confined water experimentally at the length scale of intermolecular and surface forces has, however, remained a challenge. Here we report direct molecular-level observations of hydrogen bonding in water confined inside individual carbon nanotubes (CNTs), enabled by in situ vibrational electron energy loss spectroscopy (vEELS) with nanoscale resolution. Water in larger CNTs exhibits the bonded O–H vibrations of bulk water, but at smaller diameters, and the frequency blueshifts to near the free O–H stretch found in water vapour and water located near hydrophobic surfaces, indicating a highly dispersed, non-H-bonded environment. Theoretical analysis based on quantum vibrational oscillators links the observed spectral features to local hydrogen-bonding configurations, consistent with the experimental observation. Furthermore, cryogenic experiments provide insights into complex structural phase transitions of confined water. This research reveals the quantum and dynamic nature of hydrogen bonds under confinement and the potential impact of unveiling molecular-level structure and bonding in confined fluids.

articles.title: Trade group crunches numbers on Trump’s impossible push for 100% US-made tech
articles.summary: Trump's aggressive reshoring push could cost tech firms $230 billion, CTA estimates.
articles.full_text:
One of Donald Trump’s biggest goals as president is to increase domestic manufacturing and reshore supply chains so that the most in-demand technologies in the world can be 100 percent made in the United States.
By executive order last December, he launched his “Genesis Mission,” an ambitious plan seeking to leverage US dominance in AI to maintain or seize an edge in advanced robotics, biotechnology, semiconductors, and nuclear technologies. According to Trump, that plan works best with self-sustaining supply chains. Not even neighboring countries or longtime allies should be relied upon to manufacture a single component of any US product in his ideal world.
The Consumer Technology Association (CTA) has long warned that Trump’s reshoring goals are not grounded in reality, but only recently has America’s largest technology trade association attempted to estimate what it would cost businesses and consumers to follow through on Trump’s plan.Read full article

articles.title: The Download: weight-loss drugs slowing aging and carbon dioxide batteries
articles.summary: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. articles.full_text:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.



Weight-loss drugs show signs of slowing biological aging, say drugmakers



Popular weight-loss drugs may do more than help people shed pounds. They might also slow the aging process.



Drugmakers Eli Lilly and Novo Nordisk say patients taking their GLP-1 drugs age less quickly, according to molecular “aging clocks” that track changes in DNA or levels of key proteins. 



The findings add to speculation that GLP-1 drugs could be acting on basic causes of aging and might be true longevity treatments. But how much can we read into these results?



Read the full story on what the new findings reveal about GLP-1 drugs and aging.



—Antonio Regalado



10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch: Energy Dome and its carbon dioxide batteries



Energy Dome is one of MIT Technology Review’s10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch 2026, available exclusively to subscribers.



Solar and wind are among the cheapest and quickest ways to add electricity to the grid. But they’re subject to variations in weather patterns, so supplies can be intermittent. Energy Dome has an unusual solution: massive batteries that use compressed carbon dioxide to store energy for when the grid needs it.



Compressing gas to store energy isn’t new. Utilities have used compressed air in underground caverns to hang on to reserves for decades. But Energy Dome’s approach doesn’t require any specific geology to work, so it could be more easily scaled to help grids around the world.



Here’s how the company is using carbon dioxide to store renewable energy.



—Casey Crownhart



Subscribers can now access the full 10 Climate Tech Companies to Watch, spanning everything from mobile flood barriers and electric buses to next-generation nuclear reactors.



MIT Technology Review Narrated: Don’t be fooled—LLMs don’t reason



—Thore Graepel, a core member of DeepMind’s AlphaGo team



Ten years ago, I watched a program I helped build stun the world by beating Go champion Lee Sedol. AlphaGo won after making a move so strange that some commentators thought it was a programming glitch. It was AlphaGo’s powers of reasoning that made this creative choice—and these are powers that today’s AI lacks. 



This is why I recently left my position at Google DeepMind. I believe we need a fresh approach to machine reasoning, one that draws on AlphaGo’s architecture.



This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.



The must-reads



I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.



1 OpenAI has released 377 new math findings, further rattling the fieldThey span number theory, algebra, geometry, and physics. (NYT $)+ They came from testing an unreleased OpenAI model. (Verge)+ And cost far less than its previous math breakthroughs. (SciAm)+ OpenAI also published a lengthy defense of its approach. (Gizmodo)+ AI has put mathematics at a crossroads. (MIT Technology Review)



2 Mistral says its new open-weight model is the best outside ChinaMistral Large 4 is a 1-trillion-parameter model. (Reuters $)+ Also known as le Chonk, its weights will arrive on October 27. (CNBC)+ French president Macron described it as “a third way in AI.” (TechCrunch)



3 Finland has ordered Google to halt a record data center projectThe order follows concerns over environmental impacts. (Guardian)+ The €13 billion project is Google’s largest-ever European investment. (BBC)+ But no one wants a data center in their backyard. (MIT Technology Review)



4 The EU plans to tax Big Tech through a new corporate levyThe levy would apply to companies earning more than €100 million. (FT $)+ Tesla is pushing the EU toward “Full Self-Driving” approval. (Reuters $)



5 Anduril’s $2.9 billion Navy submarine deal has sparked ethics concernsCo-founder Palmer Luckey recently joined a new Pentagon project. (CNBC)+ Anduril is also making smart glasses for warfare. (MIT Technology Review)



6 Apple is partnering with LG on a smart lock, thermostat, and doorbellApple’s new smart-home hub is expected to launch next week. (Bloomberg $)+ The companies are also co-developing security cameras. (TechCrunch)



7 The creator of a space-particle observatory has won the physics NobelFrancis Halzen used Antarctic ice to detect elusive neutrinos. (New Scientist $)



8 Drones are being used to make rain on demandThey seed clouds with silver iodide to encourage precipitation. (BBC)+ A startup claims it can stop lightning. (MIT Technology Review)



9 A new hydrogel could enable shape-shifting smart devicesThe material can evolve alongside living tissue. (SCMP)



10 You probably aren’t going to get the plagueExperts say the risk to the public remains very low. (Wired $)



Quote of the day



“I have ‘NI’—natural intelligence. I’m good with that.”



—Mike Tyran, a 66-year-old nurse and tech upgrade holdout, tells The Atlantic why he won’t swap his old gadgets for the latest AI-powered devices.



One more thing







Future AI chips could be built on glass



Human-made glass is thousands of years old. But it’s now poised to find its way into the AI chips used in the world’s newest and largest data centers. 



This year, a South Korean company called Absolics will start producing special glass panels that make next-generation computing hardware more powerful and efficient. Other companies, including Intel, are also pushing forward in this area. 



If all goes well, the technology could reduce the energy demands of chips in AI data centers—and even consumer laptops and mobile devices. Read the full story.



—Jeremy Hsu



We can still have nice things



A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)

articles.title: “Software is over”: Bold AI developer takes aim at Adobe with open source clones
articles.summary: Opus-built Creative Cloud alternatives are ambitious, free, and nowhere near finished.
articles.full_text:
For a while, those hoping to avoid the difficulty and expense of dealing with Adobe's Creative Suite have been able to use several free and/or open-source alternatives that replicate some or all of those capabilities. Now, one developer is using AI-powered reverse engineering to mimic the look, feel, and functionality of Adobe's well-known software with what he hopes will soon be perfect fidelity.
Artcraft got its start last year as a "controllable AI for artists" that allows for precise post-generation editing of AI-crafted images and videos. Over the weekend, though, the brand debuted its pivot to a suite of seven open source apps recreating the user interface and tools found in Adobe's Photoshop, Illustrator, Premiere, Lightroom, After Effects, InDesign, and Acrobat Pro.
In announcing those new apps on Reddit earlier this week, software developer Brandon Thomas said he used Anthropic's Claude Opus 5.5 to create "clean-room replacements" for Adobe's closed source software in Rust (with WebAssembly versions available for use in a browser). And while commenters on Hacker News and elsewhere have taken pains to point out the new software's many current shortcomings, Thomas make the grandiose promise that the current "super early alpha" state will soon lead to something just as functional as anything Adobe has ever put out.Read full article

PA measles outbreak tops 1,000 cases, largest since disease was eliminated
articles.summary: Pennsylvania reported 1,066 outbreak-linked cases on Wednesday.
articles.full_text:
Pennsylvania's explosive measles outbreak is now the largest the US has seen since the highly infectious virus was declared eliminated in 2000. With well over 1,000 cases, it's the largest on record since 1991.
Pennsylvania's health officials reported 1,078 measles cases in all of 2026 as of this afternoon. That includes 12 cases in January and March, with the remaining 1,066 cases since April, when the current outbreak began. The tally includes 145 cases recorded in the last seven days and 74 identified since the previous update on Monday. Health officials noted that 40 of the 74 cases added today were from more than two weeks ago and are just now being recorded.
Among the cases, there have been 207 hospitalizations and five deaths—a newborn, a 6-week-old, an 18-year-old, a 20-year-old, and a 40-year-old. All of the deaths occurred during the current outbreak in people who were unvaccinated; the two infants were too young to have been vaccinated.Read full article

articles.title: TP-Link problems in US grow amid FCC router ban and four state lawsuits
articles.summary: TP-Link can't sell latest routers in US, still needs exemption from FCC ban.
articles.full_text:
TP-Link is facing more legal troubles in the US as Florida and three other states filed lawsuits alleging that it lied to consumers about its connections to China and the risks of its routers being exploited by Chinese state hackers.
The lawsuits were filed yesterday, about six months after the Federal Communications Commission announced a sweeping ban on consumer-grade routers produced wholly or partly outside of the US. Numerous router makers have obtained exemptions to the ban, but the Trump administration so far has not granted one to TP-Link.
Router makers that received exemptions include Netgear, Asus, Adtran, Amazon and its Eero subsidiary, Calix, Nokia, SpaceX's Starlink division, and others. For now, TP-Link is unable to sell its latest Wi-Fi 8 routers in the US, though models approved before the ban can still be sold.Read full article

articles.title: Chemistry Nobel goes to reactions like those that gave life a hand
articles.summary: Altering molecular handedness has implications for the origins of life.
articles.full_text:
Life is remarkably selective. Life relies on many molecules with what is termed "handedness"—they're chemically identical but are mirror images of each other. Most chemical reactions will make a 50-50 mix of the left- and right-handed forms of a chemical, but life uses only one of them. In fact, because of the differences between left- and right-handed chemicals, most of the key enzymes used by organisms will fail to work if they're presented with chemicals that have the wrong handedness.
That poses a bit of a challenge for origin-of-life research, as we're forced to explain how a world that may have started with an even mix of left- and right-handed chemicals produced organisms that only used one of them.
Today's Nobel Prize in Chemistry goes to two individuals, Henri Kagan and Kenso Soai, who discovered chemical reactions could be biased, producing large excesses of one of the two forms of a chemical.Read full article

articles.title: Pediatricians renew call to ban raw milk as anti-science rhetoric reigns
articles.summary: In renewed policy, pediatricians review the benefits of heating milk to kill germs.
articles.full_text:
As many doctors are moving ahead with the latest advances of modern medicine—from powerful obesity drugs to breakthrough cancer treatments—pediatricians are being forced to turn back, fighting to maintain advances in children's health that were hard-won decades ago.
With anti-vaccine advocate Robert F. Kennedy Jr. as health secretary, the American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) has spent a considerable amount of time and resources in the past year fiercely defending lifesaving vaccinations—safe, routine shots that have saved the lives of millions of children over decades and thwarted untold suffering and disability.
But just this week, The New York Times reported that Ken Paxton, the attorney general of Texas, has opened aggressive investigations against pediatricians simply because they vaccinated their patients. Paxton falsely claims vaccines are part of a "multi-level, multi-industry scheme." But critics say his anti-vaccine campaign appears more aimed at currying favor with Kennedy, President Trump, and their supporters as Paxton runs for the US Senate.Read full article

articles.title: Jaguar Type 01 debuts; now, no one remembers the electric Ferrari
articles.summary: Car design sure riles people up on the Internet these days. Goes double for EVs.
articles.full_text:
Does it feel like people are perhaps a little grumpier or more on edge these days? It’s not like it’s without reason. There are wars. The climate is going haywire. Someone just died of plague. Scientific research is under attack. Machines keep stealing humans’ work. The media is a mess. And just when it all starts to feel a little overwhelming, Jaguar goes and unveils a new car.
The Type 01 is the first model to arrive from Jaguar’s rebirth. The British carmaker was an early entrant to the modern EV market with the 2017 I-Pace, which was fun to drive even if it was too small inside and perhaps completely unreliable. An all-electric sedan was supposed to be next, but a year from the showroom, it was abruptly canceled, leaving the automaker with nothing to sell as old models like the F-Pace ceased production.
Instead, Jaguar got to work on an all-new electric vehicle platform called JEA, which will underpin an all-electric product line. An elevated ownership experience and a starting price of about double the brand’s previous $60,000 entry point was the idea, Jaguar boss Rawdon Glover told me in 2024. Then last year the brand started teasing its relaunch, and everyone got upset. Things got even worse when the first images of the slab-sided and pastel-shaded Type 00 coupe concept leaked.Read full article
